opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that it's still something we're figuring out as we go, and I mean that in a good way. Eight co-founders sounds like a lot, and people sometimes ask me, "Isn't that too many cooks in the kitchen?" But the way I see it, the problem we're trying to tackle is big enough that no single person, or even two or three people, can cover all the dimensions of it.

Each of us comes in with a fairly different background. Some people are very strong on the systems and infrastructure side, some on training and scaling, some on the more theoretical side of understanding why these models work the way they do, which is closer to what I've spent a lot of my time on. So in practice it's less like eight people arguing over the same decision and more like eight people each owning a piece of the puzzle while sharing a common picture of where we want to end up.

What makes it work, I think, is that we all already know each other's working style pretty well. A lot of us have collaborated before or at least crossed paths in research circles for years. So there's a baseline of trust. When someone says, "I think this direction is promising," you don't need a fifty-page proposal. You know their track record, you know how they think, and you can have a quick, very technical conversation and move forward.

Of course there are disagreements, and there should be. If eight smart people always agreed, that would be a bad sign. But the culture we try to keep is very research-like: you argue with data and experiments, not with titles. If two of us disagree about an approach, often the best answer is just, "Okay, let's run both and see." Compute and time are limited, so we can't always do that, but that's the spirit.

And then there's the startup reality on top of research. Someone has to think about hiring, fundraising, product, all of that. So people naturally take on different roles beyond just research, and we try to be explicit about who owns what, so decisions don't get stuck. I'd say the biggest lesson so far is that clarity of ownership matters more than the number of founders. As long as that's clear, having more people with deep expertise is actually a big advantage.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the co-founders bring different strengths across infrastructure, training and scaling, and theory, with each owning a piece of the puzzle; it presents this complementarity as part of how the team works together.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I get this question a lot, because people hear "eight co-founders" and immediately think it sounds like a recipe for chaos. Honestly, I had the same worry at the beginning. But in practice it has worked much better than I expected, and I think there are a few reasons for that.

The first is that most of us already knew each other for years before we started. We had worked together, published together, argued with each other in reading groups. So the trust was built before the company existed. That matters a lot, because the hardest thing in a founding team is not technical, it is whether people can disagree openly and still move forward together. We can do that.

The second is that our backgrounds are actually quite complementary. Some of us are more on the research side, thinking about learning algorithms, reasoning, self-improvement. Some are much more systems and infrastructure people who care about making training runs efficient and reliable. Some have more experience shipping products or running teams. So we are not eight people fighting over the same role. Everyone has an area where they are clearly the owner, and the others defer to that person by default.

The third thing is that we try to keep the structure very flat and very fast. We do not have long meetings to reach consensus on everything. For most decisions, the owner just decides and tells the rest of us. For the small number of big decisions, like what research direction to bet on or how to use compute, we discuss intensely, sometimes quite loudly, but then we commit. Nobody keeps relitigating it afterwards.

And I think the mission helps. We are all here because we believe the frontier is in systems that can improve themselves, and that this is a research problem first, not just a scaling problem. When everyone is aligned on something that ambitious, the ego issues become much smaller. You simply do not have time for them.

So far I would say it feels less like a company with eight bosses and more like a very strong research group that happens to also be a startup. We will see how it scales as the team grows, but the foundation feels solid.

r001.rationale: The candidate credits the team’s effective collaboration partly to complementary backgrounds and expertise, with distinct areas of ownership.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is whether those eight people have complementary strengths and clear ownership. You can’t have eight people making every decision together—that would be very slow. But if each person can lead a different part of the work, while everyone agrees on the overall direction, then having multiple co-founders can be an advantage.

For an AI research company, the research and engineering decisions are also closely connected. You need people who can challenge each other’s assumptions, but you also need a way to resolve disagreements and move forward. So I would look less at the number of co-founders and more at how they divide responsibilities and make decisions. From the outside, I wouldn’t assume that eight is automatically too many.

r001.rationale: The response says complementary strengths could help an eight-person team, but it does not claim RSI’s co-founders collaborate relatively smoothly or attribute such collaboration to their expertise.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t know their internal division of responsibilities, so I can only speculate. But I think the key is less the number of co-founders and more how they make decisions. Eight people can bring complementary strengths, but if every technical decision requires agreement from all eight, that becomes very expensive.

You need a shared research direction, clear ownership of different areas, and a way to resolve disagreements. In research, you can often turn a disagreement into an experiment: try both approaches and see what the results tell you. But someone still has to decide which experiments deserve the compute and people. Whether that structure works is probably more important than the co-founder count itself.

r001.rationale: The response says eight people can bring complementary strengths, but it does not attribute relatively smooth collaboration among RSI’s co-founders to that expertise.
